title: Home
text:
Elias Manos
Ph.D. Candidate
Department of Natural Resources & the Environment
University of Connecticut
I am a geospatial data scientist specializing in satellite Earth observation, geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI), and spatial modeling. My research focuses on Arctic infrastructure, permafrost degradation, climate risk, and the development of scalable geospatial datasets for data-scarce regions.
My work combines deep learning, graph neural networks, computer vision, and remote sensing to characterize the built environment and assess infrastructure vulnerability across the circumpolar Arctic.
Research Interests

Arctic Infrastructure
GeoAI
Remote Sensing
Climate Risk
Permafrost
Human-Environment Systems

title: Research
text:
The estimated cost of building damage caused by projected permafrost degradation has been largely underestimated. Why? The answer is simple:

Our understanding of climate risk is only as good as our understanding of our exposure to hazards. The better we can account for what is at risk, the better we can measure risk in a changing world. Previous studies relied on geospatial building data that (1) only measured the two-dimensional area of buildings and (2) did not account for building occupancy. However, the cost of replacing a totaled (i.e., damaged beyond repair) building depends on the total floor space, not just the footprint area, as well as the purpose for which a building is designed.

After detecting buildings from satellite imagery, classifying their occupancy, and estimating the total floor space of residential buildings, projected building damage based on a geotechnical model amounts to 76 B USD under SSP2‐4.5 and 261 B USD under SSP5‐8.5.

See the methods used to map the building stock below.


The total residential floor area across the the Arctic circumpolar permafrost region amounts to an estimated 189 million sq. m, which is 75% greater than the total footprint area of residential buildings (108 milion sq. m). By mid-century, permafrost degradation could cause up to $261 billion in damage to the residential building stock.
